verifyText.value: Who must file a tax return

The IRS requires most of us to file a federal income tax return every year. In general, the federal tax agency bases its filing requirements for a given tax year on how much income you earn in a given tax filing status.
The five tax filing statuses are single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, and widow or widower with qualifying child.
For persons age 65 or older or blind, the filing requirements are a little more lenient since you can earn additional income and not have to file.

The IRS uses the following income thresholds to determine whether you must file a federal income tax return for 2023. The IRS adjusts these amounts annually for inflation so that taxpayers aren't automatically bumped into a higher tax bracket as incomes grow to keep pace with inflation:

Single taxpayers. If you expect to file a single return, the IRS requires you to file a return for 2023 if your gross income for the year is at least: $13,850 if you are under age 65. $15,700 if you are at least age 65.

Married filing jointly. For married persons filing jointly, you are required to file a return if gross income for 2023 is at least:
$27,700 if both of you are under age 65.
$29,200 if one of you was at least age 65.
$30,700 if both of you were at least age 65.

If you are not living with your spouse at the end of the year or on the date that a spouse died, the IRS requires you to file a return if your gross income is at least $5. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 repealed all personal exemptions from 2018 through 2025.
Married filing separately. For married persons filing a separate return, no matter what age, you must file a return if gross income is at least $5.

Head of household. For persons filing as head of household, you must file a return for 2023 if gross income is at least:
$20,800 if under age 65.
$22,650 if at least age 65.

Qualifying widow or widower. For persons filing as qualifying widow or widower with dependent child, you must file a return for 2023 if gross income is at least:
$27,700 if under age 65.
$29,900 if at least age 65.

Even if you don't earn this much income, other situations exist to determine whether you must file a tax return. For example, a dependent has to file a return for 2023 if they received more than $1,250 in unearned income or more than $13,850 in earned income. The amount is higher for those who are over 65 years old and/or blind. Other situations include:

You owe certain taxes. If you owe FICA or Medicare taxes (also called payroll taxes) on unreported tip or other reported income that were not collected, you must file a return. You must also file a tax return if you are liable for any alternative minimum tax. You must also file a return if you owe taxes on individual retirement accounts, Archer MSA accounts, or an employer-sponsored retirement plan.
Advance EIC payments. If your receive advance payments for the earned income credit from your employer, you must file a return.
Self-employment earnings. If your net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more, you must file a return.

Church income. If you earn employee income of at least $108.28 from either a church or qualified church-controlled organization that is exempt from employer-paid FICA and Medicare taxes, you must file a return.
For more information on the IRS's filing requirements, see IRS Pub. 17.

Tax filing status
A category closely tied to marital status that defines the type of tax return form an individual will use.
Current tax brackets
For 2024, the seven income tax rates for individual taxpayers are 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37%.

In 2024, for single taxpayers and married persons filing a separate return, the first $11,600 of income is taxed at this rate. For married persons filing a joint return, the first $23,200 is taxed at 10%. For persons filing as head of household, the first $16,550 is taxed at the 10% rate.

It helps to think of your tax rate in terms of a marginal tax rate. This is the tax rate on the last dollar of earned income that you earned. As your taxable income increases, you are taxed at a higher tax rate as a result of being bumped into a higher income tax bracket.

For example, say you file a single return and have taxable income of $50,000 in 2024. Using Table A, above, your tax liability would be $5,426.00 plus 22% of income above $47,150, or $2,850 in your case. That works out to be $627.00 for a total federal income tax liability of $6,053.00.

To prevent you from being bumped into the next-higher bracket because of a cost-of-living wage increase, the IRS adjusts upward the amount of income that can be earned for each tax bracket every year. This phenomenon of being bumped into the next-higher tax bracket is sometimes called "bracket creep."
Next, we will look at how you calculate the different definitions of income to arrive at your taxable income. Taxable income is used to calculate the amount of taxes you owe.
Calculating taxable income
When you prepare a federal income tax return such as IRS Form 1040, you calculate three levels of income: total income, adjusted gross income, and taxable income.
Taxable income is used to calculate your tax liability, the amount of federal income taxes you owe for the tax year.

Calculating taxable income is straightforward: Add up all sources of income to determine total income. Next, take any allowed "above-the-line" adjustments to calculate adjusted gross income. Finally, take any allowed deductions and exemptions to arrive at taxable income.
Total income is shown on line 9 of the 2024 Form 1040. It includes all sources of income, such as:

Wages, salaries, and tips. Income from these sources is reported on a W-2. Your employer is required to send you a W-2 by February 1, 2024. If you earn any additional income not shown on a W-2, the IRS expects you to report it voluntarily.

Interest and dividends. Banks, brokerages and other financial institutions that pay you interest or dividends mail a 1099-INT, 1099-OID, or 1099-DIV at the end of every tax year. If you earn more than $1,500 in either taxable interest or ordinary dividends, you are required to submit Schedule B with your 1040.
Capital gains. If you earn capital gains, you may have to submit Schedule D of Form 1040. See the instructions of your 1040 to see whether you have to complete the schedule.
Income earned outside of the U.S. The IRS allows you to exclude up to $126,500 (for 2024) of foreign-earned income on your tax return. For more information, see IRS Pub. 54

Social Security benefits. The IRS requires that you report some or all of your Social Security benefits as taxable income. To calculate how much to report, use the Social Security Benefits worksheet found in the instructions of your 1040.
Adjusted gross income is shown on line 11 of the 2024 Form 1040. Adjusted gross income is total income minus certain allowable deductions, including:
Contributions to IRAs. Some or all of your contributions to an IRA may be tax-deductible. For more information, see IRS Pub. 590-A.

Interest on student loans. Interest on student loans (up to $2,500) used to pay for qualified educational expenses is tax-deductible. For taxpayers filing a single return in 2024, the deduction begins to phase out when your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) reaches $75,000. The allowable student-interest deduction phases out completely when your MAGI reaches $90,000. For married taxpayers filing a joint return, the increased income limits are $155,000 and $185,000, respectively. For more information, see IRS Pub. 970.

Alimony payments. Alimony payments may be deducted from total income for any divorce or separation agreement executed prior to December 31, 2018. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 repeals the deduction for all agreements executed after December 31, 2018. For more information, see IRS Pub. 504.

Retirement and health insurance-related expenses. If you are self-employed, you may deduct from total income all of your health insurance premiums. You may also deduct contributions you make to a SEP, SIMPLE, or other small-business retirement plan. For more information, see IRS Pub. 560.
Moving expenses. You are no longer able to deduct your moving expenses if moving to take a new job for tax years 2018 through 2025 as a result of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017. See IRS Pub. 521.

Health savings account contributions. You may deduct contributions made to a health savings account. For 2024, the maximum deduction for those with family coverage is $8,300. For those with single coverage, the maximum deduction is $4,150.

Higher education expenses. For tax years 2009 through 2016, you may deduct up to $4,000 in higher education expenses if your income was not more than $65,000 ($130,000 if married filing joint). The deduction is $2,000 if your income was greater than $65,000 but less than $80,000 ($160,000 if married filing joint). This deduction was scheduled to expire after 2009 but was extended through 2016

Because tax deductions lower your taxable income, they create tax savings. The amount of tax savings is equal to the amount of the deduction times your marginal income tax rate. For example, if you're in the 25% tax bracket, every $1,000 of allowable deductions lowers your tax liability by $220.

Taxable income is the narrowest measure of income on Form 1040, which is shown on line 15 on the 2024 form. To calculate taxable income, subtract from your adjusted gross income the larger of your itemized deductions or standard deduction.
Next, we look at amounts for standard deductions for 2024.
Current standard deductions
Your standard deduction is one of the amounts you deduct from your adjusted gross income (AGI) in order to calculate your taxable income.
The larger your deduction, the lower your taxable income, and the smaller your tax liability will be.

When you file a federal income tax return (usually IRS Form 1040 or a simplified version of the form), you take either a standard deduction or you can itemize your deductions. You take the larger of the two deductions to lower your taxable income.

The IRS increases the standard deduction each year to adjust for increases in the general rate of inflation. It calculates the standard deduction by looking at the average amounts for itemized deductions that taxpayers have claimed in previous years.

However, just because you may elect to itemize your deductions doesn't always mean you should. The standard deduction is likely to be close to what your itemized deductions would be, on average, and is a heck of a lot easier to calculate.

For more information on standard deductions see IRS Pub. 501.
There are circumstances where the IRS doesn't allow you to take a standard deduction. If any of the following cases apply, you are required to itemize your deductions:
You are married and filing a separate return and your spouse itemizes deductions.
You are filing a tax return for less than a full year because of a change in your accounting period.
You were either a nonresident or a dual-status alien during the year.
Next, we take a closer look at itemizing your deductions.
Itemizing your deductions
If the amount of your allowable deductions is greater than your standard deduction, the IRS encourages you to itemize your deductions.
If you don't qualify for the standard deduction, you have no choice but to itemize. Itemizing your deductions requires you to complete Schedule A of IRS Form 1040.
For tax years 2018 through 2025, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act repealed the "Pease limitation", which phases out itemized deductions at higher incomes.
To calculate your itemized deductions, see the instructions to Form 1040.
Some major categories for itemizing deductions include:

Home mortgage interest expense. You may generally deduct the mortgage interest you pay on your residential mortgage for up to $750,000 in home-acquisition debt ($1 million for acquisitions prior to December 15, 2017). You cannot deduct the interest for home equity debt, this provision was repealed for tax years 2018 through 2025, unless the loan is used to buy, build or substantially improve the taxpayer's home that secures the loan. See IRS Pub. 936 for more information.

Private mortgage insurance (PMI). For 2007 through 2016 only, you may deduct private mortgage insurance for mortgages acquired in 2007 or after. This deduction is available in full for those with adjusted gross incomes under $100,000 ($50,000 for married filing separately). Above $100,000, the deduction begins to phase out and it is not available at all for those with adjusted gross incomes over $110,000 ($55,000 for those who are married filing separately).

Real estate taxes. Property taxes that you pay on your home may also be itemized. However, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act limits state and local income or property tax deductions for individual taxpayers to $10,000 ($5,000 for married taxpayers filing separately) for tax years 2018 through 2025. See IRS Pub. 530 for more information.

State income tax. State income tax that you pay either through withholding from your paycheck or that you pay directly to the state may be used as an itemized deduction. However, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act limits state and local income or property tax deductions for individual taxpayers to $10,000 ($5,000 for married taxpayers filing separately) for tax years 2018 through 2025.

Medical and dental expenses. Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, you may deduct qualified medical and dental expenses that exceed 10% of your adjusted gross income in 2024. See IRS Pub. 502 for more information.

Contributions to charitable organizations. The IRS allows you to deduct contributions of money or property to a qualified organization for its use. See IRS Pub. 526 for more information on the types of qualified organizations and charitable contributions.

Miscellaneous expenses. For 2017 and earlier, miscellaneous expenses are generally unreimbursed expenses that are related to your job such as travel, lodging and meals. Certain types of miscellaneous expenses can only be deducted for amounts that exceed 2% of your adjusted gross income. This deduction was repealed by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act for tax years 2018 through 2025. See IRS Pub. 529 for more information.
Next, we take a look at personal exemptions. Similar to itemized deductions, personal exemptions also phase out at higher incomes.
Taking personal exemptions
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act repealed all personal exemptions for 2018 through 2025.
Next, we take a look at some of the more popular income tax credits available for tax year 2024.
Common tax credits
Even better than a tax deduction is a tax credit. A tax credit reduces the amount of taxes you owe dollar-for-dollar. For example, a tax credit of $1,000 cuts your tax bill by the same amount.
With a deduction or personal exemption, the tax savings are only a fraction of the amount. For example, if you are in the 22% income tax bracket and have a $1,000 deduction, your tax savings is $220.
Here are some of the major categories of tax credits:

Earned income credit. the earned income credit provides a refundable tax credit to lower-income taxpayers. To qualify for the EIC in 2024, an unmarried person with no qualifying children may earn up to $18,590. (A qualifying child must pass an age, relationship and residency test.)

An unmarried person with one qualifying child may earn up to $49,083. To qualify with more than two children, total earned income may be up to $59,898. Married persons filing a joint return with three or more children may earn up to $66,818 in 2024 without losing the credit.

The Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001 provides some marriage-penalty relief by increasing the amount of income a married couple filing a joint return may earn without losing the EIC. For the three years that ended in 2004, the income phase-out limit for claiming the EIC increased by $1,000. For 2005 through 2007, it increased by $2,000. After 2007, it increased by $3,000.
If you file for the earned income credit, you must submit Schedule EIC. This can also be found in IRS Pub. 596.

Saver's tax credit. Low- and moderate-income taxpayers are eligible to take a saver's tax credit for contributing to qualified retirement plans. This tax credit provides an extra incentive to fund a retirement plan.

For single persons, the credit phases out when adjusted gross income reaches $38,250 in 2024. For married taxpayers filing a joint return, the credit phases out when adjusted gross income reaches $76,500. For heads of household, the credit phases out when adjusted gross income reaches $57,375. See IRS pub. 590-A for more information.

Child-related credits. The three major child-related tax credits are the tax credit for child and dependent care expenses, the child tax credit (not the same as the first credit) and the adoption credit. (A fourth credit, the additional child tax credit, is available for users of the child tax credit who have three or more qualifying children.)
For 2024, the maximum child tax credit per child is $2,000 for children under 17 at the end of 2024.

The adoption credit for 2024 is $16,810. You may be eligible for the maximum adoption credit even if you do not adopt a special-needs child. The 2001 tax law increased to $174,730 ($252,150 for 2024) the amount of income you may earn before the adoption credit begins to be phased out.

Education-related credits. The two main tax credits for higher education are the American Opportunity and lifetime learning credits. The Hope credit was modified by the American Opportunity Tax Credit in 2009. Those provisions were set to expire in 2017 but were made permanent by Congress as part of the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes legislation in December 2015. The maximum credit is $2,500 which is calculated by adding 100% of the first $2,000 of eligible expenses and 25% of the next $2000 of eligible expenses. Up to 40% of the credit may be refundable. The credit is phased out for taxpayers earning between $80,000 and $90,000 ($160,000-$180,000 for married filing joint taxpayers). The credit is available to students in their first four years of college.

The lifetime learning credit applies to tuition costs for undergraduates, graduates and those improving job skills through a training program. For 2024, the lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 in qualified expenses, or a maximum of $2,000. The lifetime credit begins to phase out for single taxpayers who earn more than $80,000 and for married taxpayers filing a joint return who earn more than $160,000 in 2024.

You can receive tax-free distributions from education savings accounts or qualified tuition plans without affecting your use of the American Opportunity or lifetime learning credit, provided the credit is not for the same expenses.
Distributions from education savings accounts or qualified tuition plans are excluded from your gross income for purposes of calculating the credit.

Other tax credits that are widely used include credits for elderly or disabled persons, mortgage interest credit, and a credit for refurbishing low-income housing. Next, we take a look at taxation of capital gains.
Taxes on capital gains
When you invest in stocks, bonds, and other capital assets, you may also owe capital gains taxes on the profits from the sale of those investments.
Generally, if you sell an asset at a higher price than what you paid, you earn a capital gain. If you sell at a lower price than what you paid, you earn a capital loss.
The amount of capital gain is calculated by subtracting the basis from the price for which you sell the asset. You generally add the transaction costs to buy the asset to your basis.

The length of time that you hold your investment determines whether your capital gain is treated as a long- or short-term gain. The IRS sets the cutoff period at one year. That means that if you hold a capital asset for more than one year (i.e., 366 days), the capital gain you realize on its sale is considered a long-term capital gain. Short-term capital gains are those that you earn on sales of capital assets held for one year or less.

Short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income. Long-term capital gains, however, are taxed at a preferential rate. The long-term capital gains tax rate for most investors is 15%. For single taxpayers with taxable income less than $47,025, for married taxpayers filing jointly with taxable income less than $94,055, for married taxpayers filing separately with taxable income less than $47,025, and for head of household taxpayers with taxable income less than $63,000, the long-term capital gains tax rate is 0% in 2024. For single taxpayers with taxable income more than $518,900, for married taxpayers filing jointly with taxable income more than $583,750, for married taxpayers filing separately with taxable income more than $291,850, and for head of household taxpayers with taxable income more than $551,350, the long-term capital gains tax rate is 20%.
What kinds of income do stocks, bonds, and mutual funds generate, and how is this income taxed?

Taxation on stocks. Stocks generate taxable income as dividends and capital gains. Generally, growth stocks don't pay dividends. Instead, investors expect to earn returns from an appreciation in the share price. Income stocks, on the other hand, generate regular dividend income. Since 2003, dividends have been taxed at the same rate as long-term capital gains.

Taxation on bonds. Bonds are also called fixed-income securities since they often have a fixed coupon rate. As a result, the interest income that you earn is constant over the bond term. When you sell a bond for a higher price than you paid for it, you earn a capital gain. If you buy a bond at a discount and hold it to maturity, you may earn a capital gain. If you buy a bond at a premium and hold it to maturity, you may face a capital loss.

Taxation on mutual funds. With mutual funds, taxes are a little more complicated. That's because a mutual fund distributes capital gains and dividends from the portfolio of securities it holds. Distributed short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income and distributed dividends and long-term capital gains are taxed as long-term capital gains. When you sell shares of a mutual fund for a higher price than you paid, you pay either a short- or long-term capital gains tax, depending on how long you own the shares.
Investing has other tax rules related to capital gains, including:

The "wash-sale" rule. The "wash-sale" rule is aimed at preventing investors from selling a security to lock in a capital loss, immediately buying it back at a lower price. The IRS prohibits you from using the capital loss if you buy back the same security within 30 days. To avoid being tripped up by the rule, you may wish to buy a different security that has a similar investment objective or similar risk characteristics to the one you sold.

Offsetting capital gains with losses. The IRS allows you to offset your capital gains with capital losses. If your losses exceed your gains, you can offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income in a year. If you have a larger amount of capital losses, you can carry them forward to future years. This is called the capital loss carryover rule.
For more on capital gains, see IRS Pub. 544. Next, we take a look at the Alternative Minimum tax (AMT).
Alternative Minimum Tax

The Alternative Minimum tax (AMT) was passed in 1969 to ensure that upper-income taxpayers paid at least some income taxes. Up to that point, taxpayers skilled at finding enough in itemized deductions, income exclusions, and tax credits would sometimes manage to avoid paying any income taxes.

The AMT is not without its critics, however. Most notably, critics have argued that income limits subject to the AMT have never been indexed to inflation. However, beginning with the 2012 tax year, AMT exemption amounts are now permanently indexed for inflation.

When you complete an individual income tax return such as IRS Form 1040, you will have to complete a worksheet to determine whether you owe the Alternative Minimum Tax. If you do owe, you must complete Form 6251.

The 2024 tax rate for the AMT is 26% of the first $232,600 of ordinary income that exceeds a certain exempt amount of income, shown below. The income that exceeds the exemption amount is called Alternative Minimum Tax Income. The tax rate increases to 28% for higher incomes. (For married taxpayers that file a separate return, the cutoff amount of income between the tax rates is $116,300.)

For 2024, the exemption for married taxpayers filing jointly is $133,300. For single taxpayers and heads of household, the exemption is $85,700. For married taxpayers filing a separate return, the exemption is $66,650. These numbers are now permanently indexed for inflation. Prior to 2012, Congress would generally pass an annual 'AMT patch' which raised the exemption.

The Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act (EGTRRA) of 2001 liberalized the use of the child tax credit and AMT by allowing AMT taxpayers to exclude the amount of the tax credit from their income.
Next, we take a look at the role your employer plays in withholding your federal income (FIT) and payroll (FICA) taxes.
Withholding your taxes
Your employer is required to withhold federal income (FIT) and FICA taxes from your salary or wages. FICA taxes include payments for Social Security and Medicare.

For 2024, your employer withholds Social Security at the rate of 6.2% of your first 168,600 of income. For Medicare, the withholding rate is 1.45% of your income if you earn $250,000 or less (married filing joint), $125,000 or less (married filing separate), or $200,000 or less (single or head of household). For taxpayers earning above those amounts the Medicare withholding rate is 2.35%, regardless of how much you earn.
These taxes are collected to pay for the federal government's benefits programs.
You must complete a W-4 whenever you start a new job. You should also update your withholding when you have a change in your circumstances, including:
A change in marital status, number of dependents or name.
A change in income from sources other than wages or salary.
Certain changes in wage and salary income for you or a spouse, including a second job, losing a job or changing jobs.
A change in the amount of deductions that you itemize.
A change in your tax credits.
You can submit a new W-4 with your employer at any time. For additional information, see IRS Pub. 505.

Another case in which you may face a mandatory withholding by your employer: Rolling over your retirement plan when you retire or change jobs. Under IRS rules, your employer must withhold 20% if you handle the money. This kind of transaction is called an indirect rollover. In general, using a direct rollover spares you from this withholding. You may wish to seek the advice of a professional financial or tax adviser on the options for rolling over funds from a retirement plan.

Ideally, the amount of income taxes you have withheld from your income is equal, or close to equal, to the amount of taxes you will owe for the year. If too much is withheld, a refund may be appealing but remember that a refund has a hidden opportunity cost: Instead of you earning interest on your income, you're making an interest-free loan to the IRS!

On the other hand, if too little is withheld and you're not prepared to pay at tax time, you may be forced to draw on your savings or, worse, pay with a credit card. To the extent possible, you want to optimize your withholdings to equal your estimated tax liability.

In addition, the IRS may penalize you if you have too little withheld. You're required to pay the lesser of 90% of your current year estimated tax liability or 100% (110% if your income was over $150,000) of your prior year tax liability for the year by January 15. That gives you two weeks from the end of the tax year to calculate your tax liability and check your Form W-2 to make sure you're on target. If you've withheld too little, you may complete Form 2210 to calculate your underpayment penalty.
For additional information on withholding, see IRS Pub. 505. Next, we look at how to file for an extension to complete a federal income tax return.
Filing for an extension

The traditional tax-filing deadline is April 15 every year. That means that you have until that date to file a return for the calendar year that ended 3-1/2 months earlier. For example, April 15, 2024 is the tax-filing deadline for the year ended December 31, 2023.

If you are unable to meet the deadline, you can obtain an extension by filing IRS Form 4868 by April 15. The extension extends the time to file, but not to pay. You should estimate your tax liability and send any amount you think you owe with the extension.

The extension grants you six additional months, to October 15, to file an individual income tax return. (If you are living outside of the U.S., you already have two additional months to file. In that case, submitting Form 4868 gives you an additional four-month extension.)

An extension grants you more time to file a return but it may mean paying a penalty on the amount of taxes owed but not paid at the time you file for an extension. For more information, see Form 4868.
Next, we'll look at the role of the Taxpayer Advocate Service.
Taxpayer Advocate Service
The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent service of the IRS that aims to protect your rights and interests as a taxpayer.
For an overview of your taxpayer rights, see IRS Pub. 1.
Each state and IRS service center has a Taxpayer Advocate, which is independent of the local IRS office and reports directly to the National Taxpayer Advocate.
The Taxpayer Advocate will designate an individual to provide guidance to you in dealing with such issues as:
Financial hardship you may face as a result of tax laws.
Immediate threat of adverse action as a result of tax laws.
Irreparable injury or long-term adverse impact you may face as a result of tax laws.
Handling delays of more than 30 days to resolve a tax-related issue.

The Taxpayer Advocate Service cannot reverse a legal or technical tax decision and will likely balk at frivolous claims. If you have a legitimate case, however, the Taxpayer Advocate will evaluate it for its specific merits.
You can call the Taxpayer Advocate Service at (877) 777-4778. For more information, see IRS Pub. 1546
Next, we take a look at tax audits and penalties.
Tax audits & penalties

For the 12 months ended September 30, 2021, the IRS received 167.915 million individual income tax returns with tax payments of over $12.348 trillion from individuals, according to the Internal Revenue Service Data Book 2021.

Of the 157.952 million individual returns filed in the 2021 calendar year, IRS revenue agents examined, or audited, 341,845 returns. That's 0.20 percent of all individual income tax returns filed during the year.

As these figures show, the IRS audits only a fraction of tax returns. Instead, it relies on statistical sampling, matching of statements from employers and financial institutions with individuals' statements, and other sources of public information to help identify returns for audit.

While the odds of being selected for an audit are small, it helps to keep good records and all receipts in the event you are selected for an audit. Your documents provide an audit trail that explains how you completed your tax return.
For more information on the IRS's examination process, see IRS Pub. 556.

If the IRS investigates your tax case and decides against you, you may seek to appeal the case. The first round of an appeal is likely to involve the IRS Appeals Office, which relies on an informal conference procedure. For more information on the appeals process and your rights, see IRS Pubs. 5 and 1660.
You may also wish to review the IRS's collection process, found in IRS Pub. 594. This publication describes how the IRS will impose a tax lien on your property to secure a claim.

If the IRS's appeals office rules against you, you may appeal its ruling to the appropriate judicial court: U.S. Tax Court, U.S. Court of Federal Claims, or U.S. District Court. For more information on the jurisdictions that each of these courts cover, see Pub. 5.
Finally, we take a look at e-file, the IRS's online tax-filing system for filing income tax return.
Filing a tax return online
The IRS encourages taxpayers to file their tax returns electronically using its e-file system. The online service is free, fast and reliable.
The IRS said 151.136 million taxpayers used e-file to file their returns for fiscal year 2021, surpassing the 148.157 million e-filers who used the system for the prior year returns.

According to the IRS, e-file also expedites tax refunds, shaving a week off the average time of three weeks to process a return. All fifty states and the District of Columbia participate in IRS e-file's filing program so that you may file a state tax return together with your federal tax return.
Additional features of IRS e-file include:
Security. Choose a five-digit, self-selected personal identification number (PIN) to substitute as an electronic signature using IRS Form 8879.
Accuracy. The IRS claims an error rate of less than 1% with e-file, well below an historical rate of about 20% for paper returns.

Verification. The IRS sends an electronic verification within two working days to the authorized tax professional, or electronic return originator that submits your return. (Note: Before the originator can submit your tax return with e-file, you will need to give it W-2 forms for the tax year.)

Instead of using an electronic return originator, you can also download free software from an IRS-designated Web site to send your return directly. Of the 151.136 million individual taxpayers who used e-file for the 2021 tax return season, 83.947 million returns were submitted by originators and 67.188 submitted by individuals.
A link to e-file is prominently listed in several places at the IRS Web site (www.irs.gov).
